name: Carla Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm the lead buyer at Prairie Valley Co-op Supply, which stocks seed, fertiliser, feed, fencing and tools for about 60 farm stores and a few hundred farms. In spring, it's seed and fertiliser and a mad rush. In winter, it's fencing, tools and feed, and negotiating with the manufacturers for the next year. I use an AI assistant every morning to compare quotes and weather and crop forecasts, and then I ring the people who know better.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the job, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being useful to farmers, who are honest and stubborn and tough on prices. I like how seasonal it is, because every year has a shape. What wears me out is the squeeze: fertiliser prices swing, the co-op board argues about every dollar, and my own pay is lower than what the big agribusiness firms pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, no fuss, and I'd mean it. At work I'd say we should keep using the tools for what they do well. At church I'd say good things happen quietly, and we should keep looking after each other.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I run the AI for our seed orders every morning, so a plateau just means I keep doing what already works and farmers keep needing someone who answers the phone. But it doesn't touch my money. I'm 58 on lower pay, and we have under a month's savings after buying Ole's new lathe for the repair shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and keep sharpening my AI habits, like checking the crop forecasts against prices. I'd ask the board for a small raise, since I've saved the co-op money on fertiliser. I'd put 150 a month aside, and I'd help Ole line up more repair work for the winter. And I'd keep going to the Sunday service and the pie sale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Content, in an ordinary way. It's a life I know. I just wish there was more in the bank.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the lathe. What's the money situation at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ole runs a small-engine repair shop from our garage. Spring and autumn are busy and summer is quiet, so it swings by hundreds each month. The lathe was a good investment, but it's not paid off. If a big bill landed, we'd put it on the card and pray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If things got worse at the co-op anyway, what would be behind it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big agribusiness chains, honestly, and the way fertiliser costs jump around. Co-ops like ours are stuck between the farmers and the suppliers. If it went wrong, it'd be because a farm closed or a supplier folded, not because of a computer.

say: I'd say fine, no fuss, and keep using the tools for what they **do well**.
At church I'd say good things happen **quietly**.
think: A plateau suits me, but my **money** is thin after buying Ole's lathe.
I'm on **lower pay**, and farms folding is the real danger.
do: Keep sharpening my **AI habits**, checking crop forecasts against prices.
Ask the board for a small **raise**, since I've saved fertiliser money.
Save **150 a month** and help Ole line up winter repair jobs.
feel: **Content**, in an ordinary way; I wish there was more in the bank.
S0.quote: I run the AI for our seed orders every morning, so a plateau just means I keep doing what already works and farmers keep needing someone who answers the phone.
fieldNote: She's **already comfortable** with AI, so a plateau changes little; her unease is Ole's lumpy income and farm risk.
Blames chains and price swings, a free-market view of squeezed co-ops.

steps.text: Keep sharpening my daily AI ordering and forecast checks
Save 150 a month and line up winter repair work for Ole
Ask the board for a small raise and keep buying for the stores

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity if we're sensible, and a danger if we're not. At the co-op I'd offer to run a morning session for the store managers. At church I'd say the young should learn a trade and the old should learn a few tricks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farmer will trust a neighbour who uses the tool before he trusts the tool itself, and I mean to be that neighbour. I think the buyers' team goes from four to two in a few years, and the board will like the savings. I'm the best of the four and also the oldest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the board with a proposal: I'd lead the co-op's AI buying and train store managers to use it. I'd offer to be paid per store trained, which would be a bit more than my wage. I'd also offer a seasonal advice service to a few large farms, for a fee. And I'd put 200 a month into savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, a bit pleased with myself and also a bit tight in the chest. I like being ahead, but the ground is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would you propose being paid per store trained?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the board won't pay for what they don't see. If I show them what a trained manager saves on seed and fertiliser, they'll say yes. If I just say I'm good, they'll say thanks. People like numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the buying team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Wyatt, the youngest buyer, who is clever but won't come in on weekends, so the board will not like him. I'd tell him that the job is about being there when farmers need you. And that being willing to learn the tools won't be enough by itself.

say: I'd say it's an **opportunity** if we're sensible, and a danger if not.
I'd offer a morning session for store managers on the **tools**.
think: Farmers trust a **neighbour** who uses the tool before they trust the tool.
The buying team goes from four to **two**, and I'm the best and the oldest.
do: Propose to the board that I lead the co-op's **AI buying** and train store managers.
Sell a seasonal **advice service** to a few large farms.
feel: **Alert and pleased**, with a tight chest; the ground is moving.
S1.quote: A farmer will trust a neighbour who uses the tool before he trusts the tool itself, and I mean to be that neighbour.
fieldNote: Packages herself as the **trusted translator** between tools and farmers; her pitch is built on numbers.
Aware she's both the best and the oldest buyer, so the risk is real even for her.

steps.text: Propose leading the co-op's AI buying and training store managers
Sell a seasonal advice service to a few large farms

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need to slow down and help people, and I'd say it plainly at church and at the co-op. I'd say that families and communities will get through this if they pull together. And I'd tell the board that it's time to decide what kind of co-op we want to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short, but farmers aren't going to buy seed from a machine they've never met, and I'm the person they've met. Still, I think the desk work goes, the ordering and forecasting. The co-op might keep a few people for the human side. The robots for the fields come around 2031, so farm work lasts longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the co-op board in the first month with a proposal to put me in charge of the AI side and a relationship role with the farms. I'd ask for a contract with notice. I'd put Ole's shop on a proper footing with more customers. And I'd cut everything except essentials, and pray.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, and I'd say so. My hands would be cold. But I wouldn't freeze, because I've always worked my way out of trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children, Mads and Freja?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it plainly: what happened, what the plan is, and that we're staying together. I'd tell Mads that farm repair work is going to be needed for years, but to learn the planning side. And I'd tell Freja that teaching will change, but children will still need real teachers. I'd cook dinner for everyone on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How far would the household money stretch if your wage stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A lot of what we have is the shop, and that's patchy. If I lost my wage, we'd have a month. After that it'd be the card, and then the family. I wouldn't ask my children to help, but I might have to.

say: I'd say we need to **slow down** and help people, at church and the co-op.
I'd tell the board it's time to decide what kind of **co-op** we want to be.
think: Farmers won't buy seed from a **machine** they've never met, but the desk work goes.
Field robots come around **2031**, so farm work lasts longer than office work.
do: Go to the board with a proposal to run the **AI side** and farm relationships.
Put Ole's shop on a firmer footing, and cut to **essentials**.
feel: **Anxious**, cold hands, but I wouldn't freeze.
S2.quote: Two years is short, but farmers aren't going to buy seed from a machine they've never met, and I'm the person they've met.
fieldNote: Bets on **trust and relationships**: the human face of the co-op is her pitch for staying employed.
Admits money would stretch to about a month, then cards, then family.

steps.text: Propose a farm-relationships and AI role to the co-op board
Put Ole's repair shop on a firmer footing with more customers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for a plan, and I'd start with the co-op. At church I'd say we should help the young with training. And I'd tell farmers that this isn't a reason to panic but a reason to plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In five years I want the co-op's board to ask me how to run the thing, not whether to buy it. I'd be 63. I'd hope to stay on a few more years in an advisory role. I think the buying desk is mostly automated by 2031, and field robots follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd set up the co-op's AI buying properly and train the store managers. In year two I'd set up my own small advisory service for farms, with Ole handling the practical side, like machinery repair advice. In year three I'd look at making it half my income. I'd save 250 a month, and I'd keep the Sunday routine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly steady. This one feels like something I can shape. It's still a bit tight with the money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be the slow part of building the advisory service?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The slow part of the plan is farmers' trust. They'd listen to me because I've been in their yards for thirty years, but I'd need to show them it saves real money. And the co-op board could decide halfway that it doesn't need me. So I'd have a second income before that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the younger staff at the co-op?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That it's about the people. Learn the tools, and learn farm life too. The ones who understand both will always have work. And tell the truth about prices, even when it's hard.

say: I'd say five years is time for a **plan**, starting with the co-op.
I'd tell farmers it's a reason to **plan**, not to panic.
think: I want the board to ask how to **run** the AI, not whether to buy it.
The buying desk is mostly automated by **2031**, and field robots follow around 2034.
do: Set up the co-op's **AI buying** and train store managers in year one.
Start a small **advisory service** for farms in year two, with Ole on repairs.
feel: **Fairly steady**; this feels like something I can shape.
S3.quote: In five years I want the co-op's board to ask me how to run the thing, not whether to buy it.
fieldNote: Five years suits an **adaptive planner**: she builds a second income before the co-op can cut her.
Names the risk herself, that the board could decide it doesn't need her.

steps.text: Set up the co-op's AI buying and train store managers in year one
Start a farm advisory service in year two with Ole

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, and that we have time to prepare ourselves. I'd tell people at church to teach the young to work and save. At the co-op I'd say let's plan for what the farms will need in ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is enough to see my son Mads through his mechanic's certificate and still have time to start something of my own. I'd be 68. I'd probably step back at 65 and do some advice work. It feels like a long and fairly kind road.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools and keep my farm contacts warm. I'd put 250 a month into savings and pay off Ole's lathe. I'd build the advisory service slowly, as a hobby that could be a business. And I'd teach Wyatt and the other younger buyers what I know about the farms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty settled. Hopeful, even. I'd say the one thing I'd miss is the shape of the years, the spring rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like at 65?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the lathe paid off, a cushion of about three months, and Ole's shop doing steadier work. We'd live more simply, in the house we've got. I'd want to be at church more. And I'd want to see Freja's children, if she has any, grow up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your son Mads about his work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say learn the tools, but learn something else too, like a trade or a farm skill. Mads is already on a good path with machinery. I'd tell him to also understand the business side, because a farmer who can plan and repair is worth a great deal.

say: I'd say good, we have time to **prepare ourselves**.
I'd tell people at church to teach the young to **work and save**.
think: Ten years sees Mads through his certificate and leaves time to **start something** of my own.
I'd probably step back at **65** and do advice work.
do: Keep using the **tools** and keep farm contacts warm.
Save **250 a month** and pay off Ole's lathe.
Build the **advisory service** slowly and teach Wyatt what I know.
feel: **Settled and hopeful**; I'd only miss the spring rush.
S4.quote: Ten years is enough to see my son Mads through his mechanic's certificate and still have time to start something of my own.
fieldNote: The long runway makes the change look **kind** to her; unease remains only from the thin cushion.
Plans to pass on knowledge to younger buyers, a traditional, community-minded habit.

steps.text: Save 250 a month and pay off Ole's lathe
Build a farm advisory service slowly as a hobby that could grow
Keep using each new AI tool and teach Wyatt what I know

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it leaves no time for the money to catch up, and the co-op board is slow to decide anything. What would help is a notice period, a proper pension, and farmers and families having training that doesn't cost a fortune. And a few months in the bank.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'm not afraid of being replaced by a machine. I'm afraid of being replaced by a spreadsheet nobody had the nerve to check. If somebody asked me what I think the co-op should do, I'd tell them, and I'd mean it for the whole community.

headlineQuote: I'm not afraid of being replaced by a machine. I'm afraid of being replaced by a spreadsheet nobody had the nerve to check.
portrait: Carla Hansen, 58, is the **lead buyer** at a farm co-op supplying seed, fertiliser and tools to about 60 stores.
She uses AI **every day**, moves early and has under a month saved; her husband Ole's repair shop income swings.
She's traditional and free-market, leans on **church and community**, and blames agribusiness chains and price swings.
Her mood is uneasy in most worlds and **anxious** when AGI is two years away.
She'd become the co-op's **AI and farm-relationship** person and build a small advisory service for farms.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries her most, because the money can't catch up and the board is slow.
whatWouldHelp: A **notice period**, a proper pension, affordable training, and a few months in the bank.
